title: Writing down what must be true
intro: Logic helps us separate a statement from the reasons that support it. We will start with true and false statements, then build implication, valid inference and statements about every or some object.

sections.title: 1. Give simple statements names
text: A proposition is a statement that has a truth value. Let P mean “the integer n is divisible by 4” and Q mean “n is even.” For a particular n, each statement is either true or false.
The symbol ¬ means not. The symbol ∧ means and. The symbol ∨ means or, including the possibility that both parts are true. For example, P∧Q is true only when both P and Q are true.
An interpretation assigns a truth value to each named proposition. A compound statement can then be checked from those assignments.
sections.question: Take P=false and Q=true. What are ¬P, P∧Q and P∨Q?
sections.answer: ¬P is true. P∧Q is false. P∨Q is true.

sections.title: 2. Understand what an implication rules out
text: P→Q reads “if P, then Q.” It rules out the case where P is true and Q is false. It makes no demand that P itself must be true.
For the divisibility example, n=8 makes both parts true. The number n=6 makes P false and Q true. That second case does not violate “divisible by 4 implies even.”
The expression ¬P∨Q has the same truth table as P→Q. It fails only when P is true and Q is false. This equivalence is useful when we rewrite logical statements.
sections.question: Does P→Q together with Q force P to be true? Find an assignment that settles the question.
sections.answer: No. Set P=false,Q=true. Both premises are true, while P is false. This assignment is a counterexample to the proposed inference.

sections.title: 3. Test whether a conclusion follows
text: A set of premises entails a conclusion when every interpretation making the premises true also makes the conclusion true. An interpretation satisfying the premises is called a model of them.
To disprove entailment, find one model with true premises and a false conclusion. To prove a small entailment, check all possible assignments or explain why the conclusion cannot be false.
From P→Q and P, Q follows. If Q were false while P were true, the implication would be false. This inference is called modus ponens.
sections.example: Try the same method when the premises are P→Q and ¬Q. Suppose P were true. The implication would force Q, which conflicts with ¬Q. Therefore P must be false.

sections.title: 4. Add objects and the word every
text: Propositional names describe whole statements. A predicate describes a property of an object or a relationship between objects. For example, R(x,y) might mean “person x knows person y.”
The domain is the set of objects under discussion. The symbol ∀ means “for every object in the domain.” The symbol ∃ means “there exists at least one object in the domain.”
A witness is an object that makes an existence statement true. To check ∃y R(x,y) for a fixed x, find at least one y related to that x.
sections.example: On domain {1,2}, let R(x,y) mean x=y. For x=1, y=1 is a witness. For x=2, y=2 is a witness.
sections.question: On that domain and relation, does ∀x∃y R(x,y) hold? Explain each witness.
sections.answer: Yes. For every x we can choose y=x. The chosen y can depend on x.

sections.title: 5. Quantifier order changes what is required
text: The statement ∀x∃y R(x,y) allows a different witness y for each x. The statement ∃y∀x R(x,y) requires one y that works for every x.
Using equality on {1,2}, each x has its own equal partner. But y=1 fails for x=2, and y=2 fails for x=1. No single witness works for everyone.

Negating “every object has a partner” gives “some object has no partner.” In symbols, ¬∀x∃y R(x,y) is equivalent to ∃x∀y ¬R(x,y). Move through the quantifiers one at a time and reverse every/existence when negating.
sections.example: “Every student read some book” permits different books. “There is a book every student read” requires a shared book. They are different claims even if they sound similar.

sections.title: 6. Use resolution to combine two clauses
text: A literal is a proposition or its negation. A clause is an or-statement built from literals. Consider the clauses (¬P∨Q) and (P∨R). The first says P being true requires Q. The second says P being false requires R.
Either P is true or it is false. If true, Q must be true. If false, R must be true. Therefore Q∨R must be true. This inference is called resolution on P.
The new clause is called the resolvent. It is a consequence of the original clauses. It can contain less information than both original clauses together.
sections.example: Set P=true,Q=false,R=true. The resolvent Q∨R is true, but the first original clause ¬P∨Q is false. This shows why the inference cannot simply be reversed.

remember: An implication fails only when its first part is true and its second is false.
Entailment requires every model of the premises to satisfy the conclusion.
A countermodel needs true premises and a false conclusion.
With quantifiers, ask whether witnesses may vary or one witness must work for everyone.
review: Later, translate a new everyday statement into symbols and check a proposed inference with a tiny domain. Mix implication and quantifier questions so you must decide which tool fits.
